UNESCO warns there’s close to a 100% chance of a Mediterranean tsunami | ScienceDaily Science News from research organizations UNESCO warns there’s close to a 100% chance of a Mediterranean tsunami Date: September 10, 2026 Source: ScienceDaily.com Summary: The Mediterranean may seem far removed from the world’s major tsunami zones, but history and modern modeling show that destructive waves can strike the French Riviera with surprisingly little warning. Some tsunamis could reach shore in under 10 minutes, while past events have produced waves around two meters high, powerful currents, damage, and deaths. Share: Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIN Email FULL STORY The French Riviera faces a more serious tsunami threat than many people realize, with some waves potentially reaching shore in under 10 minutes. Scientists and local officials are preparing detailed evacuation routes, refuge sites, warning tools, and public drills to help people escape before it is too late. Credit: AI/ScienceDaily.com On the French Riviera, a tsunami could arrive before a warning reaches people on the beach. In some local scenarios, the first waves could reach shore in under 10 minutes. France's national warning center, meanwhile, is designed to send its initial alert to authorities within 15 minutes of a potentially dangerous earthquake. Those two timelines leave no room for delay. That is why researchers and local officials around Nice are doing more than improving alerts. They are mapping walking routes, identifying refuge sites, and helping residents and visitors recognize when they need to leave the coast immediately. The goal is to make the first decisions before an emergency begins, rather than after the sea starts behaving strangely. What UNESCO's Mediterranean Tsunami Warning Means The Mediterranean is often treated as an unlikely setting for a tsunami. UNESCO has warned against that assumption. On June 22, 2022, the organization stated that "the probability of a tsunami wave exceeding 1 meter in the Mediterranean in the next 30 years is close to 100%." The details matter. That estimate concerned an event somewhere in the Mediterranean basin over the following three decades, roughly through 2052. It was not a prediction of an imminent disaster, a guarantee that the French Riviera would be struck, or a forecast that every Mediterranean coastline would experience the same waves. Nevertheless, the region has the ingredients needed to generate dangerous tsunamis. Earthquakes can occur along active faults in the Ligurian Sea, near the French and Italian coasts. Farther south, the movement of the African and Eurasian plates creates another source of potentially powerful earthquakes off North Africa. Underwater landslides provide an additional, sometimes much more local, trigger. The Danger Is Not Just a Giant Wave A tsunami begins when a large volume of water is suddenly displaced, often by an earthquake, landslide, or volcanic eruption. The disturbance spreads outward, potentially traveling long distances before reaching the coast. Historically called tidal waves, raz-de-marée in France or maremoti in Italy, tsunamis can bring both sudden flooding and extremely powerful currents. They do not always resemble the towering wall of water people imagine. A tsunami can appear as a rapid rise or retreat of the sea, followed by repeated surges. Flooding can range from centimeters to several meters, while fast currents can exert forces equivalent to several tons per square meter against coastal structures. The first wave is not necessarily the largest. Even relatively small tsunamis deserve attention. Italy's National Institute of Geophysics and Volcanology notes that a tsunami with an amplitude of just 50 centimeters can be dangerous because of the energy and sustained movement of the water, which can behave more like a rushing torrent than ordinary surf. Globally, tsunamis have killed more than 250,000 people since 1970. The December 26, 2004, Indian Ocean disaster and the March 11, 2011, tsunami in Japan account for much of that devastating toll. The French Riviera Has Been Hit Before The Montpellier researchers describe the Mediterranean as having the largest historical tsunami record after the Pacific. Along the French Riviera, they cite roughly 20 reported events between the 16th century and the early 2000s, including waves exceeding two meters. Several episodes show how differently the danger can unfold. On February 23, 1887, an earthquake in the Ligurian Sea, with an estimated magnitude between 6.5 and 6.8, triggered a tsunami along the coast. Historical accounts describe the sea falling by about one meter in Antibes and Cannes, leaving fishing boats stranded. Waves approaching two meters then swept over the beaches. A very different event occurred on October 16, 1979. Part of the construction site for a new commercial port in Nice (Alpes-Maritimes), beside the airport, collapsed into the sea. The resulting landslide and tsunami caused eight deaths, according to a reconstruction published in Natural Hazards . Effects were reported in Nice, Antibes, and Cannes, with disturbances observed in Antibes for about half an hour. The later study found that water reached elevations of 3.5 meters locally and flooded as far as 150 meters inland. The May 21, 2003, Boumerdès earthquake (Algeria) demonstrated that the trigger could also lie across the Mediterranean. Its effects reached the Riviera about 75 minutes later. Investigators documented abrupt sea level drops (from 50 cm to 1.5 m), partially emptied harbor basins, swirling water, strong currents, and damaged boats in eight marinas. Harbor resonance, in which the shape of a basin reinforces the water's oscillations, helped explain why neighboring ports experienced different effects. Mediterranean tsunamis are not confined to those older events. On December 4, 2022, a flow of hot volcanic material entered the sea at Stromboli and generated a small tsunami, activating the island's warning system. Italy's geological institute reported no damage, but the event provided another reminder that the region's tsunami activity is real and ongoing. Why an Alert May Not Be Enough France has operated its national tsunami warning center, the Centre d'alerte aux tsunamis (Cenalt), since July 2012. Working within the international system coordinated by UNESCO, it monitors earthquakes that could generate tsunamis and sends initial messages to French emergency authorities and other warning centers. The warning then has to reach the public. In France, the chain includes the interdepartmental crisis management operational center (Cogic), followed by authorities responsible for issuing instructions. One channel is FR-Alert, which can send notifications to mobile phones in the threatened area. Detecting an earthquake and getting people moving are therefore separate steps. Distance makes a crucial difference. A tsunami generated off North Africa may take less than 90 minutes to reach the Riviera. A nearby source in the Ligurian Sea, between Corsica and the Italian coast, can leave far less time. Local landslides are particularly challenging because their effects can develop quickly and may not be preceded by a felt earthquake. A functioning warning system cannot always overcome such a short travel time. Mapping a Way Off the Beach Planning starts with identifying where evacuation may be necessary. French government agencies and the University of Montpellier have defined a coastal evacuation zone using elevation, distance from the sea, and historical information. It generally covers land below five meters in elevation and within 200 meters of the shoreline. Around river mouths, the distance extends to 500 meters from the estuary. These are planning boundaries, not a prediction that a future wave will be five meters high. Across the French Mediterranean coast, including Corsica, that zone encompasses about 1,700 kilometers of coastline, 187 towns, and at least 164,000 residents. At the height of summer, planners must also consider an estimated 835,000 beach users. Those figures describe the scale of potential evacuation planning, not a forecast that one tsunami would affect everyone at once. In the Nice Côte d'Azur metropolitan area, dense development and heavy tourism make the challenge especially demanding. The research team used photographs and computer modeling to estimate beach attendance (between 10,000 and 87,000 people on the beaches, depending on the season and time of day). Researchers at the University of Montpellier's Laboratory of Geography and Land Planning have developed evacuation routes that account for slopes, obstacles, walking speeds, and potential bottlenecks. Rather than simply drawing a line inland, their algorithms identify the fastest walking routes to refuge sites beyond "waves' reach," which local authorities have validated. Nearly 100 refuge sites have been incorporated into operational evacuation plans. Nice Has Now Earned Tsunami Ready Recognition The preparedness effort has moved beyond a future ambition. In June 2026, UNESCO announced that the Nice Côte d'Azur metropolitan area had received Tsunami Ready recognition. UNESCO's Tsunami Ready international recognition program (TRRP) evaluates communities against 12 indicators covering risk assessment, preparedness, and emergency response. Requirements include evacuation maps, public education, an approved response plan, and reliable ways to receive and distribute official alerts around the clock. Recognition must be renewed every four years. Nice follows earlier work in Deshaies, Guadeloupe, which received recognition in 2023, and Cannes, which became the first municipality in mainland France to receive it in January 2024. Montpellier researchers provided scientific and technical support for both communities. Their methods offer a foundation for similar work elsewhere in France, Europe, and overseas territories. Maps alone, however, cannot ensure that people know how to use them. The Nice project also includes public signs, evacuation exercises, and educational activities involving schools and Montpellier students. A publicly accessible interactive platform lets people check evacuation zones, routes, and instructions before they need them. Experience in Japan shows why that preparation matters. A GNS Science review of the 2011 disaster reported a 96% survival rate among people in inundated areas and highlighted the importance of education and evacuation procedures. The same review warned that waiting too long for official information can delay escape. The Most Important Decisions Come Before the Wave A felt earthquake or unusual movement of the sea may be the first warning available. A sudden retreat can be a danger sign, but it does not happen before every tsunami. The sea may instead rise rapidly, and some local events may offer little obvious advance notice. Nice's guidance tells people in threatened coastal areas to move inland on foot toward higher ground when an alert is issued or natural warning signs appear. Drivers should stop safely and continue on foot. During an earthquake, people should first protect themselves from the shaking, then move to safety as soon as they can. The priority is to follow designated evacuation routes and local instructions, not wait for a better view of the water. Reaching safety is not the end of the response. Later waves can be larger, and dangerous currents may continue for hours. People should remain outside the evacuation zone until authorities say it is safe to return. For the French Riviera, the lesson is straightforward: an alert is valuable, but knowing where to go can be just as important. When the first wave may be only minutes away, the time to work out an escape route is before the emergency begins. Scientists find signs of extreme aging and youth in the same 117-year-old | ScienceDaily Science News from research organizations Scientists find signs of extreme aging and youth in the same 117-year-old Date: September 11, 2026 Source: Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute Summary: A remarkably detailed study of Maria Branyas, who lived past 117, reveals that extreme longevity may involve both intense aging and powerful biological protection at the same time. Researchers found signs of advanced aging, but also low inflammation, beneficial gut bacteria, protective genetic features, and a biological age younger than her chronological age. Because she avoided major disease, the study offered a rare look at aging itself rather than the illnesses that often accompany it. Share: Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIN Email FULL STORY Maria Branyas, the longest-lived person ever recorded, together with Dr. Manel Esteller, from the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute. Credit: Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute For roughly two centuries, human life expectancy climbed steadily as medicine, sanitation, nutrition, and healthcare improved. More recent research, however, suggests that this long upward trend may now be leveling off in developed countries. If that is the case, the next major challenge may no longer be simply preventing disease, but understanding aging itself. That raises a fundamental question: what actually happens to the body as it ages, and could those biological changes someday be treated in much the same way as disease? A Rare Look at Extreme Human Longevity A research team led by Dr. Manel Esteller, Head of the Cancer Epigenetics group at the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute, has now published the final peer-reviewed results from an unusually detailed study of Maria Branyas, the Catalan woman who lived beyond 117 years. Using samples collected with minimally invasive techniques, the researchers examined her biology across several layers at once. Their multi-omic analysis included genomic, proteomic, epigenomic, metabolomic and microbiomic technologies, making it the most comprehensive biological investigation yet conducted on a supercentenarian. The findings, published in Cell Reports Medicine , came from an international and multidisciplinary team coordinated by Dr. Esteller and led by Eloy Santos. Rather than finding that Branyas had simply aged more slowly across the board, the researchers uncovered a much more complicated picture. As Esteller described it, her biology showed a "fascinating duality: the simultaneous presence of signals of extreme aging and of healthy longevity." Signs of Aging Alongside Unusual Protection Some parts of Branyas's biology clearly reflected her extraordinary age. The researchers found very short telomeres (the ends of chromosomes), an immune system with pro-inflammatory characteristics, and an aged population of B lymphocytes. At the same time, other features appeared unusually favorable. She carried genetic characteristics associated with neuroprotection and cardioprotection. She also had genuinely low inflammatory levels, a gut microbiome dominated by beneficial bifidobacteria, and an epigenetic biological age that was younger than her chronological age. That combination is important because it suggests that reaching an exceptionally old age may not require escaping aging altogether. Instead, some people may experience pronounced signs of aging while also retaining biological traits that help protect against many of its harmful consequences. Clues for Blood Cancers and Age-Related Disease Aging in the blood-forming system is closely associated with a greater risk of serious and often incurable blood cancers, including leukemia and myelodysplastic syndromes. Because of that connection, the biological insights from Branyas may have implications beyond longevity research. They could also help scientists better understand how these hematological conditions develop and why some older people are more vulnerable than others. Separating Aging From Disease One of the most unusual aspects of the study was Branyas's lack of serious disease. That allowed researchers to examine the biological effects of aging with less interference from major illnesses, making this the first study in which aging could be clearly distinguished from disease in a person of such extreme age. The findings therefore offer a rare, broad view of what aging itself can do to the human body and may eventually help identify ways to counter some of those changes. Researchers caution that it is still too early to connect specific biological traits directly to particular behaviors or lifestyle choices. Even so, they point to several factors that may be worth considering when trying to understand Mrs. Branyas's exceptional longevity, including a healthy diet, a stimulating and diverse social network, and the absence of toxic habits. Could Aging Itself Become Treatable? By providing such a detailed biological snapshot of extreme longevity, the study gives researchers around the world a new reference point for investigating the aging process. Ultimately, scientists hope that a clearer understanding of aging could lead to strategies that target it directly, much as modern medicine targets specific diseases. Some of the tools needed for that effort may already exist. Epigenetic therapies and drugs designed specifically to combat senescence are already being explored in oncology, and both areas are closely connected to biological aging. It remains uncertain whether these approaches could eventually be used to extend healthy human life. But if life expectancy has truly reached a plateau, therapies aimed at the biology of aging itself could become one of the paths scientists explore in an effort to push that limit higher. Scientists discover the human heart can regrow muscle after a heart attack | ScienceDaily Science News from research organizations Scientists discover the human heart can regrow muscle after a heart attack Scientists discovered that the human heart can regrow muscle cells after a heart attack, raising hopes for future treatments that could help damaged hearts repair themselves. Date: September 10, 2026 Source: University of Sydney Summary: Researchers have shown for the first time that human heart muscle cells can regrow after a heart attack. The finding overturns the idea that damaged areas of the heart are completely incapable of regeneration. Scientists now hope to identify ways to dramatically boost this natural repair process, potentially opening a new path toward treatments for heart failure. Share: Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIN Email FULL STORY Human hearts appear to have a surprising ability to produce new muscle cells after a heart attack, according to research using living heart tissue from patients. Credit: Shutterstock Researchers from the University of Sydney, the Baird Institute and Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney have found that the human heart can produce new muscle cells after a heart attack. The discovery challenges the long-held assumption that heart muscle lost during an attack cannot regenerate and could eventually help scientists develop new treatments for cardiovascular disease. The findings were published in Circulation Research . First author Dr. Robert Hume, from the Faculty of Medicine and Health and Charles Perkins Centre, and Lead of Translational Research at the Baird Institute for Applied Heart and Lung Research, explained why the result could be important. Human Hearts Can Produce New Muscle Cells "Until now we've thought that, because heart cells die after a heart attack, those areas of the heart were irreparably damaged, leaving the heart less able to pump blood to the body's organs. "Our research shows that while the heart is left scarred after a heart attack, it produces new muscle cells, which opens up new possibilities. "Although this new discovery of regrowing muscle cells is exciting, it isn't enough to prevent the devastating effects of a heart attack. Therefore, in time, we hope to develop therapies that can amplify the heart's natural ability to produce new cells and regenerate the heart after an attack." Scientists had previously seen increased mitosis (a process in which cells divide and reproduce) in the heart muscles of mice following a heart attack. The new research is the first to demonstrate the same phenomenon in humans. The heart's natural regenerative response is not currently strong enough to replace all of the muscle destroyed during a heart attack. However, understanding how this process works could help researchers find ways to increase it. The Lasting Damage Caused by Heart Attacks Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death worldwide. In Australia, it accounts for nearly a quarter (24 percent) of all deaths. A heart attack can destroy as many as one third of the cells in the human heart. Although advances in treatment have dramatically improved survival over the past decade, surviving the initial attack does not always prevent serious long-term consequences. Many patients eventually develop heart failure, a condition in which the heart can no longer pump blood effectively enough to meet the body's needs. A heart transplant is currently the only cure for heart failure. That option is available to only a small fraction of patients. Australia has approximately 144,000 people living with heart failure, while only about 115 heart transplants are performed each year. That leaves a major gap between the number of patients who could benefit from a new heart and the number of donor organs available. Living Heart Tissue Offers a New Research Tool The research also relied on a world-first approach involving heart tissue collected from living patients during bypass surgery. These "pre-mortem" tissue samples came from consenting patients undergoing heart bypass procedures at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney. Researchers collected tissue from both diseased and non-diseased areas of the heart. The sampling technique was developed by Professor Paul Bannon and Professor Sean Lal, who work jointly at the University of Sydney, Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and The Baird Institute. Because the tissue comes from living human hearts, researchers can now study heart biology in a laboratory model that may more closely reflect what actually happens in patients. Toward Therapies That Regenerate the Heart The ability to collect and study living heart tissue could become an important tool in the search for regenerative treatments. The team hopes the model will help reveal how the heart produces new muscle cells and how that natural response might be strengthened. Professor Sean Lal, senior author of the study from the School of Medical Sciences and heart failure cardiologist at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, said: "Ultimately, the goal is to use this discovery to make new heart cells that can reverse heart failure. "Using living human heart tissue models in our work means that we will have more accurate and reliable data to develop new therapies for heart disease. "Already, our research using these samples has identified several proteins that have previously been shown to be involved in the regeneration of the heart in mice - which is a very exciting prospect to now translate to humans." Those proteins could provide researchers with clues about how to encourage damaged human hearts to generate more muscle cells. While such treatments remain a future goal, the discovery provides direct evidence that the adult human heart has at least some natural capacity to rebuild muscle after an attack. This Man Has a Cult Internet Following Over His Olive Garden Lifetime Pasta Pass | WIRED Skip to main content Save this story Save this story Everyone knows that when you’re at Olive Garden, you’re family. But in the 44 years since the casual Italian-American restaurant chain was founded, few have embraced it with the ardor that Braden Sinclair has. In fact, way back in his Little League days, a coach named him “Breadsticks.” “I had to go to Olive Garden for my birthday, ate too much, missed an entire game,” Sinclair tells WIRED. “One of my coaches decided that because of my initials being B.S., and my number being 11—which he said looked like breadsticks—and then that story, that I had to be called ‘Breadsticks’ for the rest of the season.” He maintained that close relationship with the chain for many years, until, in 2019, he was rewarded with an almost unfathomable distinction: Sinclair is one of just 50 human beings on the planet to ever secure an Olive Garden Lifetime Pasta Pass. Unlike the thousands of 13-week Never Ending Pasta Passes that the chain has offered at various intervals since 2014—this summer, a batch of 10,000, priced at $100 apiece, sold out within seconds —Sinclair’s heavy gold card bears no expiration date. It entitles him to as much pasta, toppings, breadsticks, and soup or salad as he cares to eat, for as long as the chain endures and he remains a loyal customer. (No delivery, though, to be clear. A pasta bowl so bottomless demands that one take a seat of honor for the dine-in experience.) How exactly does Sinclair wield his kingly rights at Olive Garden? All is revealed on his new website, Lifetimepastapass.com , where he crunches the many numbers—both financial and dietary—on his many meals there. And, with a continually updated poll that decides what he should order the next time he drops in, it’s easily the closest you’ll ever get to having the lifetime pass yourself. Braden Sinclair can eat unlimited pasta at Olive Garden anytime he wants. Photograph: Bonnie Durham Sinclair nabbed his license to feast during a special promotion, when Olive Garden announced that the first 50 people to buy a temporary pasta pass would have the opportunity to upgrade it to the lifetime pass for an extra $400. To this day, Sinclair wonders if his timing was really that good or if the company deliberately selected him to receive the ultimate prize. “I had sort of a joking relationship with their Instagram for years, just like chatting back and forth,” he explains, adding that it felt a little “weird” and something like “divine intervention” that he won given his coziness with the brand. An Olive Garden vice president of marketing FaceTimed him with the good news, he recalls. Reactions to the card from Olive Garden employees range from awe to confusion. “They always take it back to the kitchen, show it to people,” Sinclair says. “Managers will come out and ask questions. The other end of the spectrum has been having to kind of prove it's real, which is rare, and I totally understand. Like, if I managed a restaurant and someone came in with a gold card that said I don't need to pay, I would also have questions.” Now a 33-year-old father of two young kids, Sinclair doesn’t gorge on heaping plates of carbohydrates the way he used to (and, since frequenting Olive Garden makes him more conscientious about the rest of his diet, he’s avoided packing on the pounds). But he says the Lifetime Pasta Pass somewhat justifies his continued fixation on the restaurant, which was a familiar comfort when his family temporarily relocated from Maine to Wisconsin during his childhood. In 2016, he paid homage to the place with a tattoo of its famous rotary cheese grater; the caption reads “SAY WHEN.” He also began collecting vintage T-shirts that the chain had released in the 1980s and 1990s. This year, Sinclair unveiled the project that brought all of his Olive Garden experiences together in one place. Lifetimepastapass.com documents his “infinite tour of Italy” by showcasing not only his backstory and extensive merch collection but all the data you could ever want about how he has used his rare privilege: number of restaurant visits since 2019 (112), bowls of pasta eaten (152), calories consumed (154,817), meal value ($1,878.87) and total tips ($607.00). You can also keep tabs on a map of which locations Sinclair has tried—while the South Portland, Maine, restaurant is his home base, he has ventured up and down the Eastern Seaboard. Other charts show his most favored pasta type (rigatoni), sauce (alfredo), and topping (crispy chicken fritta), as well as the monthly frequency of his Olive Garden visits; he dined there nine times in August, the most since he set a personal record of 20 visits in October 2019, shortly after winning the pass. With a decade of experience in data analytics and visualization, Sinclair saw all this as a fun application of his talents. But he also wanted people to have “skin in the game,” as he puts it—so he built a dashboard where anyone can vote on the combination of ingredients that make up his next pasta order. “I thought it was just gonna be a joke among my friends,” Sinclair says. “You know, share it on Instagram, so maybe 10 of my friends would go in and vote, and then the next day five, and then the third day no one would care, and it would be over.” Instead, after he shared the project on a couple of subreddits, he was stunned to tally over 700 votes on his next meal. He wound up eating angel hair with spicy alfredo (a new sauce offering) and crispy shrimp fritta. “A big reason why I wanted to do this is I just kept getting rigatoni with alfredo, five-cheese marinara, and crispy chicken, like on repeat,” Sinclair says. “I was like, ‘I need to branch out.’” His best discovery so far? “I realized that alfredo and meatballs is an insane combination,” he says. “It's so good.” In some ways, Lifetimepastapass.com is a reflection of Sinclair’s belief that the card comes with great responsibility. Besides tipping diligently, he also skips the refills, aiming to be a “respectful” and “low-impact” diner who doesn’t flaunt his status or make a shift harder for staff. “I see some pictures of people with the [regular] pasta passes who go crazy,” he says. “Bowls full of grated Parmesan just because they can.” Meticulously tracking his own Olive Garden journey toward various virtual “ trophies ” earned by hitting benchmarks in categories such as “lifetime breadsticks eaten” (he’ll reach the bronze level at 100, gold at 1,000) and “longest streaks of consecutive weeks with at least one visit” seems, by comparison, a kind of reverence for the institution. If there’s an unexpected downside to the Lifetime Pasta Pass, it may be a certain loneliness at the top. Because Covid-19 hit shortly after people claimed the cards, the promotion has been largely memory-holed, and whatever plans Olive Garden could have had to celebrate or connect the winners were never realized. Sinclair has stumbled upon only a couple of other passholders via social media and has no idea how often others may go to the restaurant these days. Meanwhile, it’s not always easy to convince your pals to meet up at a restaurant just because you eat there for free. “There's only so many times I can go sit at the Olive Garden by myself,” Sinclair says. “I have some friends who are nice enough to go with me, but oftentimes they’ll just kind of sit there and eat some breadsticks.” And though Sinclair’s wife is an admitted fan of the chain—she’s eaten there with him since their high school days and promised in her wedding vows to go whenever he wants—he finds it “wisest” to seek alternatives whenever they manage a kids-free date night. The good news is that Sinclair’s 4-year-old is a likely Olive Garden devotee in the making. “I'll probably start bringing my oldest son a little more just because he's obsessed with pasta,” he says. “I think he'll genuinely enjoy it.” Just not before a Little League game, of course. I Fixed a Tractor Using John Deere’s Self-Repair Service. Farmers Aren’t Sold on It | WIRED Skip to main content Save this story Save this story There is something wrong with the tractor. The water-in-fuel sensor, a small device embedded in the John Deere machine that monitors the integrity of its diesel engine, is disconnected. And I’ve got to fix it. I’m not a mechanic or a farmer. I’m poking at a laptop at John Deere’s corporate office in Santa Clara, California. There’s a cable connecting the computer to a 5130ML tractor sitting on the grass nearby. A bright red notification sits on the screen, telling me something is wrong. I type in a question and the software pulls up instructions and a few images from the user manual that matches the serial number of the machine. Photograph: Boone Ashworth I wander over to the tractor and find the parts modeled on the screen. I spot the sensor, with two very obvious dangling wires that need to be connected together. I press them together, hear a little click, then step away and look back at the screen. The notification has cleared. Everything seems to be fine. In just a couple minutes, all by myself, I’ve fixed the water-in-fuel sensor. This fix was an easy one. It's a WiF, really. Photograph: Boone Ashworth The John Deere employees surrounding me offer their congratulations. They’ve all been very patient with me, someone who has written several articles for WIRED about their company’s seemingly steadfast reluctance to let anyone but its official technicians repair its products . In the group is Jahmy Hindman, senior vice president and chief technology officer of John Deere, who has flown in from Illinois. Hindman has worked for the company for 30 years. In that time, John Deere has thrived in an era of technological advancement. He’s here now to show off the company’s self-repair software Operations Center Pro Service , a system that pairs with nearly every electronic-enabled machine John Deere has made. “It is owner-friendly,” Hindman says. “I think that's always been our intent.” Lots of farmers would beg to differ. Oh Deere John Deere is the largest agricultural machine manufacturer in the US. In the past couple decades, machines of this ilk have become far more technologically advanced, loaded up with controllers, radios, and sensors. Many newer machines are equipped with 4G wireless connections that enable the collection of precise location data and other metrics. Some tractors can even run without a human operator at all, guided by built-in software systems to run autonomously on predetermined paths. Over the last decade, John Deere has become a big target of the ever-growing right-to-repair movement. The company’s high-tech software systems also come equipped with digital locks, which require official, dealer-sanctioned approval to access. If you want to fiddle with a part, or replace it with an aftermarket alternative, those software restrictions can block those attempts. That frustration has manifested in multiple lawsuits and even federal action. In April, the company agreed to pay out a $99 million settlement to its equipment owners to pay back burdensome repair costs. In July, the company settled a separate lawsuit brought by the US Federal Trade Commission that would require the company to make its products more repairable. John Deere did not admit wrongdoing in either case. Repair advocates say the two measures have been insufficient, both in financial terms and as requirements that will actually change Deere’s behavior. (Both settlements are not yet final until a judge issues a final ruling.) Pro Tip John Deere disagrees, of course, citing its recent efforts to make the case that its self-repair program works just fine. The company introduced its Pro Service in 2025. Prices start at an annual cost of $195 per individual machine. For bigger operations or independent repair shops, the price to access every machine in John Deere’s fleet starts at $4,995 a year. That access for agricultural and turf services costs $5,995 per year. Pro Service lets owners connect Deere’s software to their equipment via Wi-Fi or cable. Based on the serial number of the machine, the software can be used to find information from manuals and John Deere’s broader data services to diagnose any maintenance the machine needs. John Deere also recently introduced an AI chatbot called JD to its Operations Center self-repair software tool, but I did not have a chance to use that version during my visit. The AI features are meant to make it easier to find information about the components in any given machine. “As the tractor products grow in size, they also grow in number of controllers that are necessary in order to make it all work,” Hindman says, noting that in some cases tractors can have upwards of 50 controllers. “So it can be super complex.” Theoretically, Pro Service is the ultimate platform to find any equipment information and diagnose any problem. If something goes wrong, the software will guide you through a fix. Some features in Pro Service can be downloaded and used offline in case a connection isn’t working when something needs fixing. You can customize the layout to your liking and keep track of the full history of the software updates on each machine. If you need a new part, the software will helpfully serve you a link to the product in John Deere’s shop. It feels as smooth as scrolling through an Amazon page. Kelli Sullivan, a group product manager of marketing automation and governance at John Deere, is the person leading the demo. She says owners are in full control of their data and can choose whether to share it with John Deere or an independent repair shop, or keep it private. Data as a Service The thing John Deere does seem to struggle with is enticing people to use its Pro Service, or even making its customers aware of it. (That’s the reason I’m here at this demo.) A year on, John Deere says its service has about a thousand daily users —a relatively small number, given that there are somewhere around 1.8 million farms in the US. “We’re just trying to get the word out,” Sullivan says. “We have a suite of tools that are already available in our customers’ hands that allow them to do those things.” Jared Wilson is a farmer in Missouri who uses Deere machines to care for his 3,000 acres of corn and soybean crops. He is also a named plaintiff in the $99 million lawsuit against John Deere who has called that payout ruling “ fundamentally flawed .” When I describe my demo experience to Wilson, he laughs, saying the service works best on particularly simple repairs. “If you have multiple failures, you have to figure out where to start,” Wilson says. “If you have three different or four different diagnostic codes, where do you start in the tree to figure out what's wrong?” Wilson does not use Pro Service. He doesn’t know anyone who does, saying the farmers he knows tend to use cracked versions of the software they find on gray markets instead of giving their money to John Deere. Even with Pro Service, he says, farmers don’t always trust that John Deere will give farmers the tools they really need to fix their stuff. “It's taken a class action lawsuit and FTC action to get them to come this far,” Wilson says. “If you believe what they're saying now—that this is actually it and we're getting everything we've asked for—then I've got some oceanfront property in Arizona to sell you.” One of Wilson's biggest concerns with using a service like Pro Service, he says, is that it’s almost impossible to compare the dealership version of the software with the customer version of the software for parity. (Hindman says the versions of the software are all the same.) Part of the problem are PIPs, or product improvement plans, which is a term John Deere uses to identify potential or existing problems in its machines. John Deere can issue a PIP, which then goes out to let people who own a particular piece of equipment know there’s an issue with the machine. But those missives only go out after the system has gathered the information that an improvement might be needed in the first place. If a user faces a novel problem with how a machine works, it would still take time for that issue to get back to John Deere, which would verify it, then issue a PIP in Pro Service. In the meantime, the person dealing with the broken tractor won’t have the needed information to figure out exactly what is going on. Ideally, many of them would like to be able to troubleshoot the problem themselves, without having to use the company’s proprietary software. “They're still not giving us access to that next level that we have to have for some of the most difficult problems that we encounter,” Wilson says. Willie Cade, a board member of the advocacy group Repair.org and frequent critic of John Deere, takes that a step further. “They're just monopolists that want to make money and as much as they possibly can,” Cade says. “Their real customer is not the farmer. Their real customer is Wall Street.” At the demo, I ask about the repair advocates and what they get wrong about John Deere. Hindman says he doesn’t mind the pressure. “We have the best intentions of making sure that we have the ability to give customers the tools that they need to keep their equipment up and running,” Hindman says. “We share that goal in common. Are there things that we need to continue to work on? I'm sure that there are. But let's not forget that we are a long way towards moving the needle to a much better state.” The repair advocates are still pushing on John Deere. Agricultural equipment like tractors are some of the most durable goods, built to last for years and even decades of hard manual labor. If society isn’t able to establish a precedent to let people fix these machines, advocates argue, it becomes harder to pass legislation or judicial rulings that would solidify people’s rights to fix their own personal devices. “This is an issue that's concerning agricultural equipment,” Wilson says. “But it's really the vanguard of a much bigger and persistent problem that affects every aspect of our society.” Update, September 11 at noon: Additional information about the status of the two legal settlements was added to the story. These Are the Best (2026) | WIRED Skip to main content Save this story Save this story Featured in this article Best Overall Atlas Coffee Club Atlas+ Latte Superblend Read more $26 Atlas Coffee Club Best Brew for Light-Roast Lovers Bones Coffee Company Better Brain Mushroom Coffee Read more $18 Amazon Smoothest Cup of Brewed Coffee Heady Cup Mushroom Coffee Bloom Shroomery Blend Read more $33 Heady Cup Best Instant Latte Blend Bulletproof The Mood Booster Enhanced Instant Latte Read more $18 Amazon The world has been addicted to caffeine for centuries, and in the year 2026, the scientific argument over whether coffee is good or bad for you remains unsettled. One might believe the lack of consensus is a Mainstream Media™ psyop to keep people scrambling for marketable solutions to a problem that’s completely made up, but the cottage industry of coffee alternatives that’s proliferated during this endless tug of war is an interesting outcome regardless of which side you’re on. This is where mushroom coffee makes its inevitable entrance. Some quick googling revealed the known players in the game, all of which offer their own riff on a common base formula of dried mushrooms–usually a combo of lion’s mane , chaga , and cordyceps —boosted with buzzy add-ons like probiotics and nootropics. I spent a week with each, including our top pick, Atlas Coffee Club’s Latte Superblend ($26) , swapping out my morning coffee for each brand's recommended dose of powder and hot water. After day five I allowed myself to experiment with sweeteners and milks, which you’ll need with almost all of these to get through the entire cup without gagging. Photograph: Pete Cottell Some hit like a mild cup of coffee, some were actual coffee , and others were uncanny concoctions no normal person would ever crave unless they were fully indoctrinated in the heady lifestyle this unique alt-beverage industry revolves around. I laughed, I cried, I got the runs, and I crashed on my couch in the early afternoon more times than I could count, all for science, and all so you don’t have to try this on your own. Be sure to check out our other coffee and caffeinated coverage , including the Best Coffee Subscriptions , Best Coffee Makers , Best Energy Drinks , and Best Electric Kettles . Best Overall Photograph: Pete Cottell Save to wishlist Atlas Coffee Club Atlas+ Latte Superblend $26 Atlas Coffee Club As its name denotes, Atlas Coffee Club is a subscription-based mail order coffee service . And a darn good one at that! It's also our top pick in our guide to the Best Coffee Subscriptions . So when it announced it was dipping its toes in the dark arts of adaptogen-infused mushroom coffees, we trusted it could deliver the goods without all the superfluous lore and manosphere cosigns that most others come bundled with. The starter kit includes a frother and a scoop and comes with your choice of Atlas’ riffs on mushroom coffee: a coffee superblend or a latte superblend. The former is a straightforward take on mushroom-infused instant coffee. The fine powder dissolves quickly, the coffee flavor is muted with a roasty aftertaste, and only the last two sips had any amount of silty residue. If this was all Atlas offered, it would do well enough in this space. The latte superblend, on the other hand, is a real treat. Upon my opening the bag, a strong whiff of toasted coconut wafts through the room. The powder emulsifies easily in hot water without any need for a frother. Lacing on the edge of the mug is minimal, and there’s almost no gunky residue or powdery finish to speak of. The flavor of the finished product has a pronounced coconut aroma up front without the requisite sweetness that’s omnipresent in tiki drinks. The swallow offers subtle notes of earthy spice and a soft acidic tang akin to a shot of espresso pulled from Kenyan or Ethiopian beans. It’s an absolute delight to drink. After three mornings of Atlas’ latte superblend standing in for my coffee, I found myself wondering if I could permanently replace my morning brew with this delicious powder. The caffeine buzz was smooth and devoid of any mind-rattling peaks, but the probiotics did a number on my stomach on the two final days of the weeklong experiment with this one. I would not pair this with a rich, fatty breakfast loaded with eggs and dairy unless you work from home by yourself all day. Intermittent rangus aside, Atlas Coffee Club struck gold here. Best Brew for Light-Roast Lovers Photograph: Pete Cottell Save to wishlist Bones Coffee Company Better Brain Mushroom Coffee $18 Amazon Since coffee’s so-called “third wave” kicked off sometime in the early aughts, the world of light roast coffee has become a wonderland of flavor profiles and tasting notes . Conventional wisdom had adjusted accordingly, with modern consensus dictating that over-roasting beans leads to less dynamic cups that are only enjoyed by Starbucks stans, chain smokers, and gruff tradesmen. Mushroom coffee of the actual coffee variety typically lands in the medium-roast bracket for whatever reason, and on its packaging, Bones Better Brain advertises itself as such. Through some sort of unholy magic, this does not taste like a medium or dark roast in any capacity, and I mean this as a form of high praise. Gone are the common flavors of smoky bitterness and whiffs of cheap composite wood furniture on a bonfire. In their place are notes of lemongrass, citrus, and port wine, all of which you’d hope to find in a pour-over crafted from a small-batch bean from Africa or Central America. The exact milligrams of caffeine are nowhere to be found, but a 12-ounce cup of this had me tap-dancing under my desk during a busy morning filled with a four-hour block of back-to-back meetings. I brewed a smaller cup in the late afternoon before spending an hour intently watching a YouTube tutorial on a $2,700 drum machine I’m testing for another piece, and my brain processed and retained more expertise from the video—which is 3.5 hours long—than it had in any session prior. This is a wonderful beverage that I will return to even if this grand experiment comes to an end at some point. And the addition of Heady Cup Coffee Roaster’s Mushroom Coffee to the burgeoning field of mushroom-infused ground coffee—not instant coffee substitutes like most of the other entries in this list—is cause for celebration among coffee snobs who just want a nice, smooth cup of black coffee in the morning. Heady Cup ships preground as a “medium coarse” grind, which the brand recommends extracting with a French press or a pour-over. I don’t have time to babysit my coffee while it blooms and swirls in some low-tech vessel that’s not plugged into the wall, so I brewed it with the Guided Brew mode in my trusty Fellow Aiden . It was a joy to drink black, and I’m delighted to find that Heady Cup will grind your beans to your preference, which means you can order a bag that’s ready for espresso if you have a machine you like at home. Score 9.2/10 Key ingredients Lion’s mane, cordyceps Caffeine Not listed Best Instant Latte Blend Photograph: Pete Cottell Save to wishlist Bulletproof The Mood Booster Enhanced Instant Latte $18 Amazon $18 Bulletproof It’s been a wild ride for Bulletproof Coffee. What started as a quirky experiment in coffee add-ons is now a full-blown Brand that normies in Iowa can cop at Target while they shop for throw pillows and Nirvana tees for their quirked-up tweens. It was only a matter of time before Bulletproof set its sights on trendier adjuncts than MCT oil and grass-fed butter, so it’s logical that functional mushrooms made their way into the mix. Bulletproof’s Mood Booster Instant Latte is the gentler, crunchier cousin of their high-powered coffee offerings. The ad copy claims it’s free of the “earthy mushroom taste” you’ll find in competing products, and its tandem of mushroom extracts and ashwagandha aim to soften the edge of a stressful day while a light dose of caffeine staves off naptime without causing jitters. Ever since I started running a few miles a day, the paradoxical increase in energy that comes with regular cardio has decreased my need for that 2 pm quad shot of espresso to the dome, so I’ve been in the market for something exactly like this. The flavor is enjoyable, rather than simply tolerable, but calling this product a “latte” is somewhat of a reach. It contains dairy products, yet at no point did the scientifically engineered milk extracts smack me in the face with a noticeably milky texture or mouthfeel. Instead, there are vague gestures toward the idea of creaminess, looming quietly below warm notes of toasted sugar and a quick snap of stevia flavor on the finish. I generally dislike stevia in coffee drinks, but as one of many parts of this oddly satisfying composite, its position is well earned. I would not know this mellow brown elixir had even a trace of mushrooms if the package did not tell me, and I mean this as a compliment in keeping with the spirit of Bulletproof’s bold claims about this unexpected diversion in their portfolio. Atlas is still the GOAT, but until it expands its distro and appears on the shelves of big-box chain stores, this is a worthy contender that’s accessible and enjoyable for all. The Trump Alien ‘Disclosure Speech’ Rumors Are Reaching a Fever Pitch | WIRED Skip to main content Save this story Save this story In 2006, Donald Trump was firing people on The Apprentice and Dr. Phil was daytime television's reigning tough-love therapist. Twenty years later, the former is president of the United States, the latter, his informal UFO ambassador—recently trusted with unreleased government files on unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) to gauge how the public might handle what's inside. "Here's what comes in stages. First they acknowledge it, then they confirm it's real, then they tell you where it's from," Dr. Phil said in an August 7 Instagram video discussing UAP disclosure. "And somewhere down that road, maybe, is the big one—the government of the United States standing at a podium and saying out loud, we are not alone." For most of 2026, a rumor has consumed the world of UFOlogy: President Trump is sitting on a finished speech confirming humanity isn't alone. Whether the “disclosure speech” actually exists is a topic of rabid discussion on X, the r/UFO subreddit, and dozens of extraterrestrial-curious podcasts, but the reasons so many people believe in it are very real. Humans are arguably experiencing the most consequential era for the UFO scene since the ’40s and ’50s, when a mysterious crash outside Roswell, New Mexico, and unexplained radar blips over Washington, DC, birthed decades of legends of little green men and flying-saucers. There's no doubt that the government has been engaging with the topic. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently confirmed that Stephen Miller, one of the most powerful figures in the White House, has been handed the UAP portfolio. Tim Gallaudet , a retired Navy rear admiral who helped run the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration during Trump's first term, testified before Congress about UAP in 2024, and now sits on a UAP Science Advisory Council reporting to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. He called the increased government interest “a total change in executive-branch transparency from the last 80 years." But he’s unsure if that would ever culminate in a speech from a sitting president, because they would “have to acknowledge that we're not in control, that we're not the highest level of intelligence on the planet, and that's going to be a very hard thing for any government to admit." A White House spokesperson tells WIRED via email that “No such speech is planned—rather, the administration continues to release files as they become available, and the public to make up their own minds about the information uncovered.” For believers, the modern UAP disclosure began in 2017, when a New York Times article revealed a secret Pentagon program quietly investigating UAPs. The Pentagon went on to confirm in 2020 that leaked videos of Navy pilots tracking seemingly impossible objects were real. A 2021 intelligence report conceded the phenomena existed and remained unexplained, and in 2022 the government established an official investigation office . Then, from 2022 to 2025 , Congress held yearly public hearings where pilots, military officers, and intelligence veterans (including Gallaudet) testified under oath. What’s also novel is that UAP disclosure has bipartisan support. Both the House task force on declassifying federal secrets and the House UAP Caucus are made up of legislators from across the aisle. This year, the drumbeat of government interest turned into a drumroll about a potential Trump speech. In January, filmmaker Mark Christopher Lee claimed a disclosure speech was imminent , pegged to the 79th anniversary of the alleged Roswell crash on July 8. Few took him seriously. But in February, the president's daughter-in-law, Lara Trump, gave the idea new legs, saying on the Pod Force One podcast she'd heard Trump had a speech ready touching on "some sort of extraterrestrial life." Around the same time, Barack Obama mused in a podcast interview with Brian Tyler Cohen that aliens are “real” before conceding “I haven’t seen them.” Trump then accused his predecessor of disclosing classified information, and announced that he was directing agencies to release their files on "alien and extraterrestrial life." What followed was bizarre even by this administration's standards. In May, Trump posted an AI-generated image of himself escorting a handcuffed gray alien , and a mysterious loading page appeared on the domain aliens.gov , leading to rampant speculation within the UFO community that the big reveal was coming. But when the White House finally launched aliens.gov late in the month, it ended up being a Star Wars–style website that functioned as an ICE tip line—with aliens being a reference to undocumented people. The machinery of disclosure kept grinding forward. Since May, the government has released five batches of declassified videos and documents onto the Department of War's website. Detractors say the files lack context and the videos prove little . Even after the Roswell date passed, rumors about a disclosure speech intensified. In late July, Liberation Times—an independent news website with a record of breaking UAP stories —reported that a speech confirming some UFOs are of non-human origin had been prepared for Trump . The site’s founder, Christopher Sharp, tells WIRED the story began with a call from a source he deeply trusts. "They basically said, ‘Look, I'm quite shaken, because it looks like Trump may make some kind of announcement on UAP disclosure’." Another source described the speech itself, he says, alleging it basically reads, “we're not alone, we have captured some of these or retrieved some of these things, they're of non-human origin, and that there is a reverse engineering effort." Sharp was also told Trump wouldn't deliver it unless unspecified conditions were met. "If you're the president, you have to be sure that there's firm evidence," he says. "The worst thing you can do is come out with this speech and then whatever you put out could be debunked straight away ... You'll go down in history as a laughingstock." In August, the rumor hit a fever pitch. Robert Bigelow, the billionaire aerospace mogul who has bankrolled UFO research for decades and once owned Utah's infamous Skinwalker Ranch (a 500-acre plot of land renowned for alleged alien and paranormal activity and later the namesake of a popular History Channel series), told veteran Las Vegas journalist George Knapp that he'd met Trump in the Oval Office months earlier and personally handed him a speech containing a single sentence: "A non-human, intelligent presence has been on Earth for a very long time, using spacecraft and with performances completely beyond our capabilities and our human physics.” Bigelow said he advised the president to deliver the line casually, on his way to boarding Air Force One—no evidence, no press conference, just confirmation. Trump hasn't said it. Yet. If the cycle of presidents and UFO disclosure feels familiar, that's because it is. For nearly 80 years, someone has always supposedly been on the verge of revealing the truth, but no president has ever delivered. "Politicians overpromise," says Greg Eghigian, a professor of history and bioethics at Penn State and author of After the Flying Saucers Came . "The reality is that even presidents are not privy to a lot of classified information that lies within the bowels of the military and intelligence community bureaucracy." Still, for the believers, the stakes justify the hope. “Often in the mainstream, when this topic gets brought up, there's a giggle factor. I can tell you who is not giggling about this: senior members of the administration, senior intelligence officials, senior members of the military, senior members of Congress,” says Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation , a nonprofit that advocates for UAP transparency. “When the door closes, no one ever says, ‘Oh, this is all made up, isn't it?’ No. The door closes and they say, ‘We know there's something happening here, we know this is serious, what do we do about it?’" But that discourse still hasn’t been confirmed, at least in a meaningful way to the general public. "A speech from the President of the United States confirming the existence of things in our airspace that we do not understand would unequivocally contribute to the public taking this issue seriously," says Flowers. Eghigian, however, isn't so sure a Trump pronouncement would settle anything, particularly from "this president, who has a long history of not telling the truth." If the past is any indicator, this could be another nothingburger. “Unless something radically different happens, which I know a lot of people are counting on, what we could probably expect is that this will eventually die down,” he says, citing an 80-year history of “intense moments where societies are really focused on the subject, and then all of a sudden interest wanes, and then all of a sudden it appears again." Right now, interest is arguably at anall-timee high. Few politicians enjoy a public spectacle as much as Trump, and what spectacle could be bigger than news that transcends our planet, and potentially our galaxy. Maybe the rumor just becomes another footnote on presidents and UFO lore. Or maybe it becomes the most important proclamation in human history, delivered by a reality TV star, with a talk show shrink by his side. How 9/11 Made Everyone a Conspiracy Theorist | WIRED Skip to main content Save this story Save this story There are many, many strange things about the stew of conspiracy theories that fall under the umbrella of “9/11 Truth”—the false, often antisemitic worldview purporting that the US government had inside knowledge of or even actively participated in the September 11 attacks. But perhaps the strangest is that the seed of these theories was planted three months before the attacks themselves. It was June 28, 2001, when Milton William “Bill” Cooper took to the air on his national radio show after watching a news report on CNN. “Supposedly, a CNN reporter found Osama bin Laden, took a television camera crew with him, went into Osama bin Laden's hideout, interviewed him and his top leadership, his top lieutenants and colonels and generals in their hideout,” Cooper told his listeners. “He came out and told everybody, ‘Within three weeks, Osama bin Laden is going to attack the United States and Israel.’” Cooper had part of the story right—a reporter had indeed just reached the inner sanctum of al Qaeda in the mountains near Kandahar, Afghanistan, but he was actually a correspondent for a Middle Eastern broadcaster. And that reporter, the MBC correspondent Baker Atyani, had actually interviewed al Qaeda’s military chief, Mohammed Atif, not bin Laden. “In the coming weeks, there will be a big surprise; we are going to hit American and Israeli installations,” Atif told Atyani. “The coffin business will increase in the United States.” According to Atyani , bin Laden—who was present for the interview—smiled and nodded. To Cooper, speaking on the radio that day, the interview represented either a major embarrassment for the US government, which had been hunting bin Laden for years, or it was evidence that the government was lying about the threat from bin Laden. “Now, don’t you think that’s kind of strange, folks?” Cooper said. “The largest intelligence apparatus in the world, with the biggest budget in the history of the world, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and can't find him. The FBI, also under the leadership of Louis Freeh, has been looking for Osama bin Laden for years and years and years and years and years and many years and can’t find him. Some doofus jerk-off reporter with a camera crew waltzes right into his hideout and interviews him?” “Now that tells us two things: Either everyone in the intelligence community and all of the intelligence agencies of the United States government are blithering idiots and incompetent fools, including the entire apparatus of the FBI and all of their personnel—or they're lying to us. They're not looking for him at all.” Cooper went on to say that “the CIA created Osama bin Laden” and that “they're now using him to help bring about world government by making him the big boogeyman because they can't use [Iraqi dictator] Saddam Hussein anymore.” Cooper argued that the whole threat from bin Laden was a farce—what would now be called a “false flag” operation. “If you believe it, you are one of the stupidest jerks that ever lived on the face of this earth, and whatever’s going to happen they’re going to blame on Osama bin Laden.” About 10 weeks later, Cooper’s comment would come to be seen as a prophecy. The events and aftermath of 9/11 altered almost every aspect of American society: from the ever-present security theater of daily life—the 3.4-ounce liquid bottles at airports, the defensive bollards that now dominate so many urban landscapes—to the expansion of the surveillance state, to 20 years of war in Afghanistan, to the backdrop of fear and anxiety that permeates the culture. Few, though, rightly recognize one of the most important and pernicious impacts of 9/11: how it changed our society’s very understanding and relationship to facts and truth. It’s a story that not many people fully understand, one with roots in the UFO conspiracies of the 1980s and with tentacles that stretch to the National Mall on January 6, 2021—and one that helps in particular to explain the transformation of Alex Jones from a fringe Austin, Texas, talk show host to one of the most important (and disruptive) political forces of the 21st century. This transformation began in the first minutes after the September 11 attacks. Cooper first came to prominence in the 1980s, among the first of a group who would come to be known as “UFO whistleblowers,” former military or intelligence veterans who purported to have insider knowledge about the government’s cover-up of alien civilizations, captured spacecraft, and recovered alien life-forms. It was the first golden age of modern conspiracism, as trust in government cratered following Vietnam, Watergate, and the revelations of dark assassination plots by the Pike and Church committees; books about cover-ups and urban legends like the Bermuda Triangle and the “ Philadelphia Experiment ” became bestsellers. Cooper claimed to have been a naval intelligence officer in the 1970s and said that, as part of his work with a high-ranking admiral, he’d been able to covertly paw through the contents of the admiral’s cabinet of classified material. As Colin Dickey wrote in a review of a Cooper biography, the cabinet became “a repository of secrets known only to Cooper, whose contents seemed to change and evolve over the years, fitting whatever need Cooper’s current conspiracies had.” In early iterations, Cooper hinted it contained the truth about the JFK assassination and the government’s contact with aliens. In the 1990s, amid the rise of far-right talk shows like that of Rush Limbaugh, Cooper became a national radio figure as well; his shortwave The Hour of the Time focused on a witches’ brew of sinister government conspiracies, alternate histories, warnings about the New World Order and secret societies, and a healthy dose of general-purpose skepticism; Cooper often exhorted his audience, “Wake up, sheeple!” (Much of his conspiracism contained thinly and not-so-thinly veiled antisemitism.) For a brief period, Cooper was one of the nation’s most famous “UFO-ologists,” but few believed him—he feuded frequently with others in the field. He eventually laid out a grand conspiracy account in his 1991 memoir/fever-dream of a book, Behold a Pale Horse. Behold a Pale Horse is a wacky piece of writing—there’s almost no other word for it. At one point it quotes the entire text of the Protocols of the Elders of Zion , a fabricated antisemitic screed from the early 1900s that alleged a secret Jewish plot to overthrow Christianity. Cooper’s work was basically QAnon three decades early, outlining a vast global conspiracy, decades-long and all-encompassing, to steal America and our freedoms from real Americans, all to serve some global super elite. The book became an underground bestseller—it still is today—and took off particularly within the militia movement. This newfound fame coincided with the start of his talk radio career on WWCR, World Wide Christian Radio, in January 1993. With a 100,000-watt signal, he could reach huge swaths of the country from his home in Arizona. And over time, Cooper developed two important—and later infamous—superfans. One was a young Gulf War veteran named Timothy McVeigh, who in the early spring of 1995 journeyed with a companion—their exact identity is disputed—to Arizona to try to talk to Cooper at his home. “The last thing he said before they left in their green Mercury Marquis station wagon with a puke-yellow interior was, ‘Watch Oklahoma City,’” Cooper would later recount. Soon after their meeting, McVeigh attacked the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building, killing 168 people and injuring nearly 700. Then there was Alex Jones, a local public-access talk show host in Austin, Texas, who first came onto the national radar for his fundraising work to rebuild the church at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas. The site had burned down in 1993 at the end of a 51-day siege by the US government, as federal agents tried to arrest the leader of the Branch Davidian cult, David Koresh. In the end, agents in armored vehicles tried to fill the compound with tear gas; the buildings caught fire—it was never clear how the fires started—and most of the Davidians who remained in the compound died in the blaze. There were 75 fatalities, including about two dozen children. The Waco siege was a key flashpoint for the far right in the 1990s. Jones saw inspiration in Cooper’s model, and Cooper became something of a mentor to the budding radio host, calling in for an interview on Jones’ early shows. Jones’ show on KJFK-FM lasted until 1999—he was even voted “Best of Austin” radio host by a local newspaper, which called him “either Austin’s great exposer of truth or a black helicopter conspiracy nut, depending on your worldview.” But his conspiracism made getting sponsors difficult, and KJFK fired him in December 1999. Jones quickly latched on to a new venture on the expanding internet: Infowars.com. On September 11, 2001, Cooper was outraged by the attacks and warned of what would come next. “Folks, I can assure you that 72 hours from now, we will be at war. We will be bombing two or maybe three countries … Because that’s how it works. When governments are attacked, they lash out. Thousands of people who had nothing whatsoever to do with what is happening at the World Trade Center and the Pentagon are going to die,” Cooper said. “Nothing will be the same after today.” Broadcasting that day on Infowars and about 100 syndicated stations, Jones did one better: “I went on the air and said, ‘Those were controlled demolitions,’” he later told Rolling Stone. In the weeks ahead, Cooper and Jones diverged politically. Cooper had come to see Jones as a copycat, a fearmonger, and a liar. (On September 26, 2001, Cooper’s show was titled simply “Alex Jones—Liar.”) Amid the aftermath of the September 11 attacks, Jones dove deeper into budding 9/11 conspiracies, and Cooper—who had stopped paying taxes, was drinking heavily, and was engaged in sometimes violent disputes with his neighbors—began prophesying his own death. In November 2001, law enforcement arrived at his Arizona compound to arrest him on an outstanding warrant on suspicion of aggravated assault; Cooper opened fire, shooting one deputy in the head, and was killed in the returning police gunfire. The field was clear for the rise of Alex Jones. In the years that followed, Alex Jones became a key force in the spread of 9/11 conspiracies. The movement, which came to be known as “9/11 Truth,” encompassed a host of different theories: that United Airlines Flight 93 had been downed by US fighters; that the Pentagon had been struck by a missile, not a plane; that the World Trade Centers had been brought down by space weapons. By even the first years after 9/11, the ideas had become so widespread that the government’s 9/11 Commission took pains to document in careful factual detail the impossibility of some of the conspiracies, hoping to avoid the ambiguities that dogged the Warren Commission’s report into the JFK assassination. Popular Mechanics devoted a special issue—later turned into a book, with a foreword by Senator John McCain—to debunking the most popular ones. But the conspiracies took root in the early internet of the 2000s: Arguably the first viral online documentary, known as Loose Change , took the conspiracies to the broader public, becoming one of the most-watched videos on Google Video and the early era of YouTube. (Jones would even get an “executive producer” credit on one version of the film.) The DVD box promised, “What you will see inside will prove without a shadow of a doubt that everything you know about 9/11 is a complete fabrication.” The reality is that the film offered no conclusive evidence of government involvement or conspiracy, but would be familiar format-wise to anyone online today in its “We’re-just-asking-questions” tone, c
